name: T. Rowe Price Capital Appreciation Fund
strategy: Active balanced fund (~60% stocks, plus bonds, convertibles, and cash) run by David Giroux; closed to new investors outside certain channels.
best_for: The lucky investors who already have access — it's largely closed (note: the fund is closed to new investors; existing shareholders can still add)
editorial: PRWCX is the active fund that index-fund writers bring up when they want to seem fair, because the record is absurd: under David Giroux it has beaten its category in essentially every rolling multi-year period for nearly two decades, with a flexible stocks-bonds-convertibles mandate executed with unusual discipline. If skill exists in mutual fund management, the strongest evidence files live here.

The catches are instructive. It's closed to new retail investors precisely because Giroux protects the strategy from asset bloat — the same bloat that broke Magellan — so most readers can't buy it anyway. The fee, 0.72%, is a high hurdle that the fund has so far cleared. And the whole thesis rests on one manager's continued tenure; the day Giroux retires, owners will face the exact succession gamble Contrafund holders face. Keep it if you have it. The inaccessibility is, perversely, part of why it works.

name: T. Rowe Price Blue Chip Growth Fund
strategy: Active large-growth fund concentrated in dominant franchise companies — historically heavy in mega-cap tech and consumer names.
best_for: Growth investors loyal to the T. Rowe research bench
editorial: For most of the 2010s, TRBCX was the argument for active growth investing: a concentrated book of franchise compounders that lapped the index year after year. Then 2021–2022 happened — the fund fell dramatically harder than the Russell 1000 Growth and gave back years of accumulated edge in months. The full record now reads as a high-beta growth bet: glorious in expansions, punishing in growth bears.

That's not a scandal; it's the honest shape of concentrated growth investing, and T. Rowe's analyst bench remains genuinely strong. But an investor choosing between TRBCX at 0.70% and a Russell 1000 Growth index fund at 0.035% is paying twenty times the fee for the chance that concentration helps more than it hurts going forward. The last decade's evidence on that question cuts both ways, which — for a 20x price — is not a ringing endorsement.

name: T. Rowe Price Growth Stock Fund
strategy: Active large-cap growth investing in companies with durable earnings growth; one of the oldest growth funds in America.
best_for: Mostly legacy holders; new growth money has cheaper options
editorial: Founded in 1950 by Thomas Rowe Price himself — the man who more or less invented growth-stock investing as a discipline — PRGFX is a piece of living market history. Seventy-five years of compounding through every regime is no small thing, and the fund remains a competently run, diversified large-growth portfolio.

History, though, doesn't discount the fee. At 0.65% against index alternatives at a twentieth of that, PRGFX needs persistent stock-picking edge in the most efficient, most-analyzed corner of the global market, and its recent decade against the Russell 1000 Growth doesn't demonstrate one. Legacy holders with embedded gains have tax math on their side; new money has FSPGX and VIGAX. Mr. Price, who preached adapting to change, might well agree.

name: T. Rowe Price Equity Income Fund
strategy: Active large-value investing in established dividend payers trading below intrinsic value.
best_for: Traditional dividend-value investors who want a human at the wheel
editorial: PRFDX is classic Old Wall Street value: buy sturdy dividend-paying companies when they're out of favor, collect the income, wait for sentiment to revert. Brian Rogers ran it that way for three decades; his successors run it the same way. It does what it promises — a value-tilted, income-generating large-cap portfolio with below-market downside in most drawdowns.

The question is the same one every competent active fund faces: VVIAX delivers the large-value style for 0.05%, VHYAX delivers the dividend screen for 0.08%, and PRFDX charges 0.67% to deliver a human-curated blend of both. Over most trailing periods the index pair has been the better deal after fees. The fund isn't bad — it's priced for an edge the category rarely sustains.

name: T. Rowe Price Dividend Growth Fund
strategy: Active investing in companies with the ability and commitment to grow dividends over time; quality-tilted large-cap portfolio.
editorial: PRDGX hunts the same prey as Vanguard's dividend-appreciation index — companies that reliably raise payouts — but with analysts making the calls instead of a screening rule. The result is a quality-heavy portfolio that has historically cushioned bear markets well and kept pace respectably in bull markets, one of the steadier records in active large-cap land.

Steadiness, however, is exactly what the index version sells for 0.08%. The 0.56% fee gap means PRDGX's managers must out-pick a dividend-growth screen by more than half a percent annually, forever, just to tie. Some years they have; over long stretches the race is close enough that the cheaper fund wins by default. If you want this style with active cover, it's among the more defensible choices — but 'more defensible than most active funds' is a low bar this site keeps having to mention.

name: T. Rowe Price New Horizons Fund
strategy: Active small/mid-cap growth investing in emerging companies, including pre-IPO positions; closed to new investors.
best_for: Existing holders only — closed, and a study in small-cap capacity limits
editorial: New Horizons is one of the legendary small-cap growth funds — six decades old, an early backer of countless companies before they were famous, and under Henry Ellenbogen's 2010s tenure, the rare fund whose pre-IPO sleeve added real, measurable value. It closed to new investors years ago, which is both a disappointment and the responsible move: small-cap alpha dies of asset bloat faster than any other kind.

For the readers who hold it: the post-Ellenbogen era has been rockier, with the 2022 growth unwind hitting hard, and the fund's size forces it ever further up the cap spectrum from its small-cap roots. For everyone else, the lesson generalizes nicely — when an active fund is good enough to be worth buying, it's usually closed, and when it's open to you, ask why. Index funds never face this paradox; VSGAX takes all comers at 0.07% precisely because it isn't trying to be clever.

name: T. Rowe Price Health Sciences Fund
strategy: Active healthcare sector investing across pharma, biotech, devices, and services.
best_for: Investors who insist on a healthcare bet and want specialist management
editorial: If there's a sector where active management has a fighting case, healthcare is it: binary FDA outcomes, scientific complexity that genuinely rewards expertise, and T. Rowe's health team has a long record of navigating it better than the sector index more often than chance would suggest. PRHSX has been one of the better sector funds in existence over multi-decade windows.

The site-house-view caveat still applies twice over. First, sector funds are concentration by definition — your total-market fund already holds healthcare at ~13% weight, so this is a doubling-down, not a diversifier. Second, sector enthusiasm is procyclical: money floods into healthcare funds after great runs and leaves after droughts, and the gap between fund returns and investor returns in sector funds is among the widest measured. A small, permanent, never-traded slice is the only version of this fund that tends to work as well as its chart.

name: T. Rowe Price Retirement 2040 Fund
strategy: Actively managed target-date fund of T. Rowe funds, de-risking toward 2040 with a comparatively equity-heavy glide path.
best_for: 401(k) participants whose plan offers this series — with a fee caveat
editorial: T. Rowe's Retirement series is the strongest brand in *active* target-date funds, common in 401(k) menus, and it has two genuine distinctions: a more aggressive glide path that holds more stocks later than rivals (a defensible response to longevity risk), and underlying active funds from a deep research shop. Its long-term results against active TDF peers are very good.

Against the index target-date series, though, the fee gap is the whole story: roughly 0.59% versus 0.08–0.12% means this fund starts every year half a percent behind Vanguard, Schwab, and Fidelity Index equivalents, compounding over a forty-year accumulation into a five-figure difference on an ordinary balance. The aggressive glide path can be replicated for free by just picking a later-dated index fund. If TRRDX is your plan's only target-date option, it's far from a disaster — but if an index series sits next to it on the menu, the math has a clear favorite.

name: T. Rowe Price Retirement 2050 Fund
strategy: Actively managed target-date fund of T. Rowe funds, de-risking toward 2050; currently around 90% equities.
best_for: Younger savers defaulted into T. Rowe-administered 401(k) plans
editorial: Millions of workers own TRRMX because their employer's plan is administered by T. Rowe Price and this is the default — which makes it worth saying plainly: as defaults go, this is a good one. Diversified, equity-rich for the horizon, professionally rebalanced, and run by a firm whose active funds are better than average. A young saver auto-enrolled here is being treated decently.

Decently, but not cheaply. The ~0.61% expense ratio is the toll for active underlying funds, and over 25 years it compounds into real money versus an 0.08% index series. The practical advice: contribute happily to TRRMX while it's your plan's best option, capture every employer match — and when you change jobs, roll the balance to an IRA where the index target-date series cost one-seventh as much. The glide path travels; the fee doesn't have to.
